questions.q: An analyst needs read access to exactly one table inside a shared lakehouse, and nothing else in the workspace. What's the correct control?
options: A OneLake data access role scoped to that table's folder
Promote the analyst to workspace Contributor
Share the entire lakehouse item with the analyst
Duplicate the table into a brand-new lakehouse just for them
questions.explain: A OneLake data access role scopes access to specific folders/tables inside one lakehouse, without touching workspace role or duplicating data (Fabric Lesson 60).

questions.q: A warehouse table with a 'Confidential' sensitivity label feeds a report that gets exported to Excel by an authorized user. What happens to the label?
options: It persists on the exported file — sensitivity labels travel with the data
It resets automatically because exports leave the workspace boundary
It only applies inside the original warehouse table, never downstream
It converts into a workspace role automatically
questions.explain: Sensitivity labels are Purview-backed and attach to the data itself, per Fabric Lesson 61 — they travel through reports and exports rather than resetting at any boundary.

questions.q: What does a workspace role (Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer) actually control?
options: What a person can do across every item in that one workspace
Which rows of a specific table a person can see
Whether a sensitivity label survives an export
Access to one specific item without touching the rest of the workspace
questions.explain: Workspace roles are the broadest layer, granting or restricting access to everything in the workspace (Fabric Lesson 2) — item permissions and data access roles narrow it further.

questions.q: Where does row-level security (RLS) actually apply in a Fabric solution?
options: Inside a semantic model — it filters which rows a given user sees
At the lakehouse folder level, identically to a OneLake data access role
At the workspace level, replacing the need for workspace roles
It applies only to KQL databases, never to semantic models
questions.explain: RLS is a semantic-model concept (Fabric Lesson 13), separate from lakehouse-level OneLake data access roles — a scenario asking about lakehouse table access needs a different control.

questions.q: A scenario asks for the narrowest control that satisfies an access requirement, and lists a workspace role change as one option. Why is that usually the wrong answer on DP-700?
options: Because a workspace role grants access to every item in the workspace, which is broader than most scenarios require
Because workspace roles don't actually exist in Fabric
Because workspace roles can only be set by Microsoft support
Because workspace roles apply exclusively to Eventstreams
questions.explain: The recurring DP-700 trap in this domain is a real but too-broad control; the correct answer is almost always the narrowest control that still satisfies the scenario.

questions.q: What's the difference between an item permission and a OneLake data access role?
options: Item permission grants access to one whole item; a data access role scopes access further, to folders/tables inside that item
They are two names for the exact same feature
Item permission is more granular than a OneLake data access role
A data access role replaces the need for a workspace entirely
questions.explain: The access-scoping ladder narrows step by step: workspace role, then item permission, then OneLake data access role, then RLS at the row level inside a semantic model.

questions.q: Which practice covered in Fabric Lesson 63 is most relevant when a governance scenario asks about removing access someone no longer needs?
options: Access reviews and least-privilege — periodically re-checking who has what, and trimming what's no longer needed
Sensitivity labeling, which has nothing to do with removing access
Row-level security, which only adds access rather than removing it
Capacity planning, which is unrelated to access control
questions.explain: Fabric Lesson 63 covers access reviews and least privilege directly — the practice of periodically confirming access is still needed and removing what isn't.
